entries.title: Enterprise guide
entries.summary: Production topics the System Design Primer does not cover, split into short decision-oriented pages.
entries.when_to_use: Use when you are designing or reviewing a real system and the Primer chapter stops at the interview sketch.

entries.title: AI systems
entries.summary: Placeholder for LLM application architecture, retrieval, agents, security, and evals.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a design includes an LLM, a retrieval index, an agent, or an evaluation of model output.

entries.title: Contract testing
entries.summary: Check producer and consumer agreements in CI so a shared staging environment is not the only integration test.
entries.when_to_use: Use when two deployables share an API or an event and can ship on different days.

entries.title: API gateways
entries.summary: Put edge concerns at the gateway and keep product policy in the service that owns the data.
entries.when_to_use: Use when many clients enter through one front door and you are deciding what that door is allowed to do.

entries.title: Rate limiting
entries.summary: Choose a limiter algorithm from whether bursts are allowed, and key it on the identity that should pay the cost.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a caller can send work faster than you intend to serve it, including your own jobs.

entries.title: REST, gRPC, and GraphQL
entries.summary: Pick one style per boundary from who the caller is, whether the shape is stable, and who pays for round trips.
entries.when_to_use: Use when two components must talk and you are choosing the contract style.

entries.title: API versioning
entries.summary: Evolve contracts compatibly, and introduce an explicit version only when a break is unavoidable.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a caller you do not deploy in lockstep depends on an API or an event.

entries.title: Webhooks
entries.summary: Sign each delivery, retry with backoff, and make the receiver dedupe on an event id.
entries.when_to_use: Use when your system must notify a customer or a partner about an event and they cannot or will not consume your log.

entries.title: Tamper-evident audit logs
entries.summary: Record privileged actions in an append-only log that operators cannot quietly edit, and keep it separate from debug logs.
entries.when_to_use: Use when an admin action, a data export, a permission change, or a security-relevant read must be provable later.

entries.title: HIPAA and PCI DSS basics
entries.summary: Shrink the systems that touch PHI or cardholder data, and put the extra controls only on what remains.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a design might store or transmit protected health information or payment card data and you need the architectural consequences.

entries.title: GDPR and CCPA basics
entries.summary: Inventory personal data, minimize it, and build export and deletion as product paths rather than as tickets.
entries.when_to_use: Use when the system stores information about people, including customer employees, and you need the engineering consequences of privacy law.

entries.title: Data residency
entries.summary: Pin a tenant's data, backups, and operator access to the regions the contract allows.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a customer or a law requires data to stay in a country or region, or when you replicate across regions by default.

entries.title: Retention and deletion
entries.summary: Give every store a retention period and a deletion path that includes indexes, vendors, and backups.
entries.when_to_use: Use when data is stored for more than the request that created it, including logs, backups, and derived indexes.

entries.title: SOC 2 basics
entries.summary: Treat SOC 2 as an attestation that named controls operated over a period, and build the evidence those controls need.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a customer asks for SOC 2 or when you are deciding which operational controls a product system must emit evidence for.

entries.title: Cost allocation
entries.summary: Attribute shared spend to teams and tenants with tags and a written split, so showback is explainable.
entries.when_to_use: Use when more than one team or tenant shares a platform and someone asks who spent the money.

entries.title: Capacity planning
entries.summary: Turn the traffic estimate into a resource plan with headroom, a lead time, and a date to revisit.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a launch, a tenant move, or a 10× concern needs more than a guess that the cloud will autoscale.

entries.title: FinOps
entries.summary: Make spend visible to the teams who cause it, and review it on a cadence with the same seriousness as an SLO.
entries.when_to_use: Use when cloud or vendor spend is large enough that a surprise invoice is an incident.

entries.title: Unit economics
entries.summary: Express cost per business unit so a design change can be compared to the revenue or the budget it serves.
entries.when_to_use: Use when you need to know whether a feature, a tenant, or a plan tier pays for the infrastructure it consumes.

entries.title: Change data capture
entries.summary: Stream committed database changes from the log when consumers need the row-level history the database already committed.
entries.when_to_use: Use when another system must follow committed changes and you cannot or should not add an outbox to every write path.

entries.title: Event-driven architecture
entries.summary: Publish facts that already happened, let consumers build their own state, and treat delivery as at-least-once.
entries.when_to_use: Use when several services must react to a change and the producer should not call each of them in the user request.

entries.title: Data governance
entries.summary: Assign an owner, a classification, a lineage, and an access rule to data people will rely on.
entries.when_to_use: Use when more than one team produces or consumes a dataset, or when personal or regulated data is copied out of the system of record.

entries.title: Idempotency
entries.summary: Make a retried request return the original result, and reject the same key when the body differs.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a client, a queue, or a saga may send the same write more than once and a duplicate effect would be wrong.

entries.title: Sagas
entries.summary: Split a multi-service business transaction into local steps plus compensations, and choose a choreography or an orchestrator.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a user action must update several services that do not share a database transaction.

entries.title: Schema evolution
entries.summary: Change events and tables so old and new producers and consumers overlap for at least one release.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a stored record, an event, or an API payload will change and more than one deployable reads or writes it.

entries.title: Transactional outbox
entries.summary: Write the business change and the message you must publish in the same database transaction, then publish asynchronously.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a service must update its database and publish an event, and either side failing alone would corrupt the other service's view.

entries.title: Warehouse and lakehouse
entries.summary: Keep operational stores for transactions, and land analytical copies in a warehouse or a table format on object storage.
entries.when_to_use: Use when people need historical, cross-cutting queries that must not run on the transactional database.

entries.title: CI and CD
entries.summary: Build an artifact once, test it, sign it, and promote that same digest through environments.
entries.when_to_use: Use when code must reach production through a path you can explain, reverse, and audit.

entries.title: Database migrations and rollback
entries.summary: Change schemas in expand and contract steps so the previous application version still runs, and so rollback does not require time travel.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a release changes a table, index, or constraint that an older binary might still touch.

entries.title: Feature flags
entries.summary: Separate release from deploy with short-lived flags, and make the off state safe when the flag service is down.
entries.when_to_use: Use when you need to ship code dark, open it to a subset, or kill a path without a redeploy.

entries.title: Infrastructure as code and environments
entries.summary: Describe infrastructure in reviewed code, and keep environments separated without copying production personal data downhill.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a cloud resource, network rule, or environment difference can exist and you need it to be reviewable and repeatable.

entries.title: Progressive delivery
entries.summary: Expose a release to a small slice first, watch the SLO, and expand or roll back on that evidence.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a production deploy can hurt users and you can shift traffic in steps.

entries.title: Authorization models
entries.summary: Choose RBAC, ABAC, or ReBAC for the decision, and enforce it on the server from the authenticated identity.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a caller is already authenticated and you must decide whether that caller may perform an action on a resource.

entries.title: OIDC and OAuth 2.0
entries.summary: Pick an OAuth 2.0 flow, bind tokens to the right audience, and treat OpenID Connect as the identity layer on top.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a person or a first-party app needs delegated access to an HTTP API, or when you must know who the user is.

entries.title: SSO and SAML
entries.summary: Accept enterprise single sign-on through SAML 2.0 when a customer IdP requires it, and keep the assertion checks strict.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a customer's identity provider can only speak SAML, or when you are the identity provider for a partner that requires SAML.

entries.title: Secrets management
entries.summary: Keep secrets in a manager, inject them at runtime, scope who can read them, and rotate them without a redeploy heroics story.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a workload needs a credential, key, or token that must not appear in source, images, or logs.

entries.title: Service-to-service auth
entries.summary: Give every workload an identity and a short-lived credential, using workload identity, SPIFFE, or mutually authenticated TLS.
entries.when_to_use: Use when one service, job, or pipeline calls another and no human is in the request.

entries.title: Anti-corruption layer
entries.summary: Translate between a legacy model and a new model in one place, so the new model does not grow the legacy system's concepts.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a new component must talk to a legacy or external system whose model you do not want to adopt as your own.

entries.title: Modular monolith
entries.summary: Keep one deployable, split it into modules with hard boundaries, and extract a service only when a team or a scale number requires it.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a codebase is growing and a microservice split is the proposed cure, before you have a team or an operational reason to split.

entries.title: Strangler fig
entries.summary: Put a seam in front of the legacy system and replace one capability at a time until the old path can be deleted.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a legacy system must stay in production while you replace it, and a rewrite-from-scratch cutover is too risky.

entries.title: Alerting and on-call
entries.summary: Page a named owner on user-visible symptoms that threaten the error budget, and keep a human rotation that can act.
entries.when_to_use: Use when you are deciding what wakes a human up versus what waits for the next business day.

entries.title: Incident response
entries.summary: Declare early, assign roles, mitigate first, and keep a timeline that the postmortem can trust.
entries.when_to_use: Use when user impact is underway or likely, and ad-hoc chat is no longer enough to coordinate.

entries.title: OpenTelemetry
entries.summary: Instrument with OpenTelemetry and put sampling, redaction, and vendor export in the collector, not in application code.
entries.when_to_use: Use when you are adding or replacing instrumentation and want one pipeline for traces, metrics, and logs.

entries.title: Blameless postmortems
entries.summary: Write what happened, why the system allowed it, and which actions will change the system, without blaming a person.
entries.when_to_use: Use after a SEV-1 or SEV-2 incident, a near miss that would have been one, or any customer-impacting data incident.

entries.title: SLIs, SLOs, and error budgets
entries.summary: Define a user-visible indicator, set a target over a window, and spend the error budget on purpose.
entries.when_to_use: Use when you need to say how reliable a feature must be and how you will notice it is not.

entries.title: Logs, metrics, and traces
entries.summary: Use metrics for symptoms and alerts, traces for one request's path, and logs for the detail you cannot aggregate.
entries.when_to_use: Use when you are deciding what a service should emit so an on-call engineer can tell whether a user request succeeded.

entries.title: Conway's law
entries.summary: Expect the system to mirror team communication, and change the team boundary when you want a different system boundary.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a proposed service split does not match how teams talk, or when a reorganization is about to redraw the architecture by accident.

entries.title: ADRs and RFCs
entries.summary: Use an RFC to shape a proposal with the people it affects, and an ADR to record the decision you actually made.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a choice will be expensive to reverse, or when a later reader will otherwise relitigate it in a pull request.

entries.title: Service ownership
entries.summary: Give every service and store one owning team that ships it, runs it, and answers for its data.
entries.when_to_use: Use when more than one team touches a system and you need to know who is paged and who may change the schema.

entries.title: Platform teams
entries.summary: Run an internal platform as a product with customers, a golden path, and a support model that is not a ticket black hole.
entries.when_to_use: Use when several product teams would otherwise each build CI, clusters, observability, or tenancy primitives.

entries.title: Team topologies
entries.summary: Organize teams by the kind of work they do and the way they are allowed to interact, so delivery is not an accident of the org chart.
entries.when_to_use: Use when you are splitting people around a system and need more than 'everyone owns everything' or 'one team per microservice.'

entries.title: Reference architectures
entries.summary: Four end-to-end designs with requirements, estimates, a diagram, tradeoffs, and a severity-ranked design review.
entries.when_to_use: Use when you want a worked design to compare against, not a blank template.

entries.title: Reference architecture: data platform
entries.summary: CDC from operational databases into a lakehouse with owned curated tables, deletion, and a catalog.
entries.when_to_use: Use as a baseline when analytical workloads must leave the transactional database and personal data still has to be deletable.

entries.title: Reference architecture: event-driven orders and payments
entries.summary: Checkout as an orchestrated saga: authorize payment, reserve inventory, then capture, with an outbox and idempotent provider calls.
entries.when_to_use: Use as a baseline when an order must update payments and inventory without a single distributed transaction.

entries.title: Reference architecture: internal platform with SSO and audit
entries.summary: An internal developer platform with corporate SSO, a service catalog, and a tamper-evident audit log.
entries.when_to_use: Use as a baseline when an internal control plane must know who changed production and must use the corporate identity provider.

entries.title: Reference architecture: multi-tenant B2B SaaS
entries.summary: A pooled work-management SaaS with a bridge tier for large tenants, SSO, and tenant-scoped webhooks.
entries.when_to_use: Use as a concrete baseline when designing a multi-tenant business application with shared infrastructure and a few dedicated tenants.

entries.title: Chaos testing
entries.summary: Run a small, reversible fault with a hypothesis and an abort switch, and write down what broke.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a failover, timeout, or shedder exists on paper and you need evidence it works before an incident does.

entries.title: Circuit breakers and bulkheads
entries.summary: Stop calling a dependency that is failing, and isolate its concurrency so it cannot sink the whole process.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a dependency can be slow or down and callers would otherwise pile up work waiting on it.

entries.title: Disaster recovery, RPO, and RTO
entries.summary: Name how much data you can lose and how fast you must be back, then test the restore that those numbers require.
entries.when_to_use: Use when you must survive zone, region, or data-corruption events and a backup policy is being treated as a plan.

entries.title: Load shedding
entries.summary: Reject excess work early, with a clear retry signal, before the process collapses under queueing delay.
entries.when_to_use: Use when traffic can exceed capacity faster than you can scale, or when one class of request must be sacrificed to keep another alive.

entries.title: Multi-region architectures
entries.summary: Choose active-passive or active-active from the RPO, the RTO, and whether two regions may write the same key.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a single region outage is in scope and you are placing reads, writes, and data replication.

entries.title: Retries, backoff, and timeouts
entries.summary: Bound every remote call with a timeout, and retry only idempotent work with jittered backoff.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a caller depends on a network hop that can be slow, dropped, or temporarily unavailable.

entries.title: Encryption and key management
entries.summary: Encrypt in transit and at rest with managed keys, separate data keys from key-encryption keys, and do not invent a cipher.
entries.when_to_use: Use when data moves across a network or sits on disk, in a backup, or in a queue, and you must decide who can read it.

entries.title: OWASP ASVS chapter map
entries.summary: Point a design at the ASVS 5.0.0 chapter that covers the control, without copying the standard's requirement text.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a review or a design must name the security control area for an API, token, session, or data store.

entries.title: Software supply chain
entries.summary: Know what you build, produce an SBOM, sign the artifact, and deploy only what you verified.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a pipeline builds an artifact that production will run, or when you take a dependency you did not write.

entries.title: Threat modeling with STRIDE
entries.summary: Walk the data flows once per trust boundary and name spoofing, tampering, repudiation, disclosure, denial of service, and elevation of privilege.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a design introduces a new trust boundary, a new data store, or a new kind of caller, before you treat the design as ready to build.

entries.title: Zero trust
entries.summary: Authenticate and authorize every request, and treat network location as an untrusted hint.
entries.when_to_use: Use when you are deciding whether a private network, a VPN, or a security group is enough of a control for an internal system.

entries.title: Per-tenant data and keys
entries.summary: Put the tenant on every record and decide which tenants get their own encryption key.
entries.when_to_use: Use when you are choosing a primary key, a cache key, or a KMS key strategy for a multi-tenant store.

entries.title: Tenant isolation models
entries.summary: Pick silo, pool, or bridge isolation per tier of tenant, and write down what a bug in one model can leak.
entries.when_to_use: Use when more than one customer will share a deployment and you must decide what they share.

entries.title: Tenant onboarding and offboarding
entries.summary: Provision a tenant as a record plus policy, and offboard it including access, exports, deletion, and backups.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a customer is created, suspended, moved, or closed and you must say what happens to identity, data, and spend.

entries.title: Noisy neighbors
entries.summary: Cap one tenant's load so a shared pool stays fair, and move a tenant to a silo when caps are not enough.
entries.when_to_use: Use when tenants share a database, cache, queue, or worker pool and one tenant's spike can slow the others.

entries.title: Tenant-aware routing
entries.summary: Resolve the tenant from the credential and the host, then send the request to that tenant's home region or cell.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a request must land on a specific tenant's data placement, cell, or regional deployment.

entries.title: What's dated in the Primer
entries.summary: Where the System Design Primer's advice shows its era, and the current equivalent to use in a design.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a Primer section is the starting point and you need to know what not to copy literally into a new system.

entries.title: Enterprise system design skills
entries.summary: Tool-agnostic architect, design-reviewer, and ADR-writer skills, with the references and worked example they ship with.
entries.when_to_use: Use when installing these skills into Cursor or Claude Code, or when choosing which skill runs next.

entries.title: Complementary sources
entries.summary: License-checked index of works the Primer does not cover, and whether each one may be copied into a skill.
entries.when_to_use: Use before citing SRE, ASVS, twelve-factor, Well-Architected, or microservices.io, so the license is settled before any text is copied.

entries.title: Worked example: multi-tenant audit log
entries.summary: A hand-run of the architect and design-reviewer skills on one multi-tenant audit log, including where the review disagrees with the design.
entries.when_to_use: Use when you want a finished example of the skill output instead of the procedure alone.

entries.title: Multi-tenant audit log design
entries.summary: Architect-skill design for a multi-tenant audit log, covering ingest, tenant-scoped search, export, retention, and the capacity arithmetic.
entries.when_to_use: Use when you want to see the system-architect sections filled in for a production feature.

entries.title: Multi-tenant audit log review
entries.summary: Design-reviewer findings on the multi-tenant audit log, led by the missing erasure path and the single-writer hash chain.
entries.when_to_use: Use when you want to see severity-ranked findings against a design that already looks complete.

entries.title: adr-writer
entries.summary: Use this when recording an architecture decision: context, the decision, alternatives rejected and why, consequences, and status, as an Architecture Decision Record.
entries.when_to_use: Use this when recording an architecture decision: context, the decision, alternatives rejected and why, consequences, and status, as an Architecture Decision Record.

entries.title: When to write an ADR
entries.summary: Choose an ADR to record one decision already made, an RFC while several teams still have to critique an open choice, and a design doc for the whole system.
entries.when_to_use: Use when you are about to record a choice and need to decide whether it is an ADR, an RFC, or a section of the design doc.

entries.title: ADR template
entries.summary: The canonical Architecture Decision Record outline: status, context, the decision, rejected alternatives, and consequences.
entries.when_to_use: Use when copying the outline for one architecture decision into the place your team keeps ADRs.

entries.title: design-reviewer
entries.summary: Use this when reviewing a proposed software architecture or system design for production gaps: single points of failure, cache invalidation, consistency, 10x load, failure modes, authentication and authorization, OWASP ASVS, compliance, observability, retention, cost, migration, and team boundaries.
entries.when_to_use: Use this when reviewing a proposed software architecture or system design for production gaps: single points of failure, cache invalidation, consistency, 10x load, failure modes, authentication and authorization, OWASP ASVS, compliance, observability, retention, cost, migration, and team boundaries.

entries.title: Design review checklist
entries.summary: Ordered review questions from single points of failure through ownership, plus the ASVS 5.0.0 chapter names used as citations.
entries.when_to_use: Use when walking a proposed design for production gaps, one checklist section at a time.

entries.title: system-architect
entries.summary: Use this when turning a feature or product request into an enterprise system design: functional and non-functional requirements, back-of-the-envelope traffic, storage, and bandwidth estimates, a mermaid component sketch, a data model, an API outline, and explicit tradeoffs.
entries.when_to_use: Use this when turning a feature or product request into an enterprise system design: functional and non-functional requirements, back-of-the-envelope traffic, storage, and bandwidth estimates, a mermaid component sketch, a data model, an API outline, and explicit tradeoffs.

entries.title: Design method
entries.summary: The four-step design method adapted from the Primer, and the section headings a written design has to emit.
entries.when_to_use: Use when turning a request into a design and you need the step order and the output sections.

entries.title: Data, consistency, and availability
entries.summary: How to pick a store, a consistency model, and a replication scheme, with the Primer's older terms mapped to current names.
entries.when_to_use: Use when the design has to name a database, a consistency choice, or what a failover does to writes.

entries.title: Enterprise checks for a design
entries.summary: Production decisions the architect writes as requirements before the sketch, covering identity, tenancy, retention, operability, cost, and migration.
entries.when_to_use: Use when the system-architect skill is writing requirements for a system that will run in production.

entries.title: Estimates
entries.summary: Back-of-the-envelope formulas plus the Primer's powers-of-two, latency, and availability figures used for capacity math.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a design needs a shown rate, storage, bandwidth, latency budget, or availability product.

entries.title: Scaling patterns
entries.summary: When cache, shard, CDN, queue, and load-balancing patterns apply, including Primer notes that no longer match current practice.
entries.when_to_use: Use when an estimate shows a bottleneck and the design must name the pattern and its cost.

entries.title: Pattern cards
entries.summary: One card per pattern with the problem, when to use it, when not to, tradeoffs, and failure modes.
entries.when_to_use: Use when you already know the pattern name and need the operational decision, or when you are choosing among a small set of options.

entries.title: Anti-corruption layer
entries.summary: Translate between a new model and a legacy or external model so foreign concepts stay at the edge.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a new component must integrate with a system whose model should not become your model.

entries.title: API gateway
entries.summary: A single edge that authenticates, limits, and routes requests, without owning product decisions.
entries.when_to_use: Use when many clients share a front door and you want TLS, authentication, and routing in one place.

entries.title: Availability and failover
entries.summary: Stand up a second copy and a tested promotion path so one failure does not end the service.
entries.when_to_use: Use when the availability target is tighter than a single machine or a single zone can honestly meet.

entries.title: Backend for frontend
entries.summary: A server-side API shaped for one client, aggregating downstream services so the client does not.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a specific client (web, mobile, or a partner) needs a different aggregation or auth cookie story than the domain APIs provide.

entries.title: Blue/green
entries.summary: Run two complete environments and switch traffic from the live color to the idle one.
entries.when_to_use: Use when you can afford a second full stack and you want to cut back to the previous version quickly.

entries.title: Bulkhead
entries.summary: Give each dependency or tenant a separate concurrency limit so one failure cannot take every thread.
entries.when_to_use: Use when one process calls several dependencies or serves several tenants and a slow one must not exhaust the shared pool.

entries.title: Cache-aside
entries.summary: The application reads the cache, and on a miss loads the store and fills the cache.
entries.when_to_use: Use when reads repeat, the source of truth is a database, and a short staleness window is acceptable.

entries.title: Cache invalidation
entries.summary: Define who may overwrite or delete a cached entry and the maximum staleness a caller can observe.
entries.when_to_use: Use whenever a cache or derived index exists. Invalidation is part of adopting the cache, not a follow-up.

entries.title: Canary
entries.summary: Send a small fraction of traffic to the new version and expand only if the user-visible metrics hold.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a bad deploy should hurt a small slice first and you have a metric that will show it.

entries.title: Change data capture
entries.summary: Read committed row changes from the database log and stream them to other systems.
entries.when_to_use: Use when consumers need the committed row stream and you cannot add an outbox to every writer.

entries.title: Content delivery network
entries.summary: Serve cacheable bytes from a location near the user so the origin does not see that request.
entries.when_to_use: Use when many users fetch the same bytes and those bytes can be stale for a TTL you name.

entries.title: Circuit breaker
entries.summary: Stop calling a dependency that is failing, fail fast for a cool-down, then try a few probes.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a dependency can be down or slow and callers would otherwise pile up threads waiting on timeouts.

entries.title: Consistency patterns
entries.summary: Choose weak, eventual, or strong consistency per path, and write the partition behavior separately from the healthy-path latency.
entries.when_to_use: Use when more than one copy of data exists and a reader might not see the latest write.

entries.title: CQRS
entries.summary: Use a write model shaped for commands and a read model shaped for queries, updated asynchronously.
entries.when_to_use: Use when the read shape and the write shape fight each other, and read staleness is acceptable.

entries.title: Denormalization
entries.summary: Store a copy of a field next to the data that reads it, so a hot path does not join.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a measured read path is too slow or too frequent because of a join, and you can name how the copy stays fresh.

entries.title: Event sourcing
entries.summary: Store the state of an aggregate as an append-only sequence of domain events and derive current state by fold.
entries.when_to_use: Use when you must keep the history of changes itself, not only the latest row, and you can operate projections.

entries.title: Feature flags
entries.summary: Branch behavior at runtime so you can ship code dark, open it gradually, or turn it off without a redeploy.
entries.when_to_use: Use when deploy and release should be different events, or when a path needs a fast kill switch.

entries.title: Federation
entries.summary: Split databases by function so each domain has its own store and its own write path.
entries.when_to_use: Use when different domains have different load or ownership, and joins across them can become application calls.

entries.title: Idempotency keys
entries.summary: Store the result of a write under a client-supplied key so a retry returns the same result and does not repeat the effect.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a client or a worker may send the same write more than once.

entries.title: Load balancing
entries.summary: Spread requests across healthy targets so one instance is not the user-facing capacity or the single failure.
entries.when_to_use: Use when more than one instance serves the same stateless role, or when you need health checks to remove a bad instance.

entries.title: Load shedding
entries.summary: Reject new work when the service is past a defined saturation point so accepted work can finish.
entries.when_to_use: Use when traffic can exceed capacity faster than scaling can react.

entries.title: Message queues and async processing
entries.summary: Accept work onto a durable queue and let a worker finish it after the user request returns.
entries.when_to_use: Use when the user does not need the result to complete the action, and the work must survive a process crash.

entries.title: Rate limiting
entries.summary: Count or meter requests per identity and reject the excess before the service is overloaded.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a caller, tenant, or job can submit work faster than its allowance.

entries.title: Refresh-ahead
entries.summary: The cache reloads a hot entry before its TTL expires so the next reader does not pay for a miss.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a small set of keys is predictably hot and a miss would spike latency.

entries.title: Leader-follower replication
entries.summary: One leader accepts writes and replicates them to followers that serve reads.
entries.when_to_use: Use when read traffic exceeds one node's capacity and you can tolerate replication lag on the read path.

entries.title: Multi-leader replication
entries.summary: More than one node accepts writes, and the nodes converge, with conflicts when they write the same key.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a single writer is an availability problem you have measured, and you have a conflict rule.

entries.title: Retry with backoff
entries.summary: Repeat a failed idempotent call with exponential delay and jitter, and stop at a budget.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a call can fail transiently and repeating it does not double the side effect.

entries.title: Reverse proxy
entries.summary: A proxy in front of the origin terminates client connections and can cache, compress, and hide the origin.
entries.when_to_use: Use when you want TLS termination, request limits, static file serving, or a single front for one or more origins.

entries.title: Saga
entries.summary: Complete a business transaction as a series of local commits with explicit compensations.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a user action updates several services that do not share a transaction.

entries.title: Sharding
entries.summary: Split one dataset so each node holds a subset of the keys, usually by hash or by range.
entries.when_to_use: Use when one dataset's size or write rate no longer fits one primary, and the access pattern is by a shard key.

entries.title: Sidecar and service mesh
entries.summary: Run a helper beside each instance, or a node-level proxy plus optional waypoints, when many services need the same mTLS and traffic policy.
entries.when_to_use: Use when many services need the same transport security and traffic policy and you will actually operate the mesh.

entries.title: Strangler fig
entries.summary: Route capabilities one at a time from a legacy system to a new one behind a stable facade, then delete the old path.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a system must be replaced in production and a single cutover is too risky.

entries.title: Transactional outbox
entries.summary: Commit the business write and the outbound message in one database transaction, then publish asynchronously.
entries.when_to_use: Use when you must update your database and notify another system without a dual write.

entries.title: Write-behind
entries.summary: The application writes the cache and the store is updated asynchronously after the caller has been told success.
entries.when_to_use: Use when write latency must be tiny and you can lose or delay the latest writes if the cache dies.

entries.title: Write-through
entries.summary: The application writes the cache and the cache writes the store before the write returns.
entries.when_to_use: Use when reads must see the latest write and you can spend latency on the write path.

entries.title: Templates
entries.summary: Copyable templates for a design doc, an ADR, a threat model, an SLO, a runbook, a postmortem, and a capacity worksheet.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a human or an agent is about to write one of these documents and should start from a fixed outline.

entries.title: ADR template pointer
entries.summary: The canonical Architecture Decision Record template lives with the adr-writer skill. Copy that file, not a second variant.
entries.when_to_use: Use when you are about to record one architecture decision and need the outline.

entries.title: Capacity estimate worksheet
entries.summary: A worksheet for request rate, bandwidth, storage, the first bottleneck, and the cost driver.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a design needs back-of-the-envelope numbers that a reviewer can recompute.

entries.title: Design doc template
entries.summary: Outline for a system design with requirements, estimates, a component sketch, data, API, and tradeoffs.
entries.when_to_use: Use when turning a request into a design another engineer can review.

entries.title: Postmortem template
entries.summary: A blameless incident write-up with a timeline, impact, contributing factors, and owned actions.
entries.when_to_use: Use within a few days of a severe incident or a near miss that would have been one.

entries.title: Runbook template
entries.summary: The steps on-call follows for one page, including how to tell that the mitigation worked.
entries.when_to_use: Use when an alert is being added and a human will be asked to act.

entries.title: SLO template
entries.summary: A one-page definition of an SLI, its target and window, and what happens when the error budget burns.
entries.when_to_use: Use when a service needs a reliability target that alerting and release policy can share.

entries.title: Threat model template
entries.summary: A STRIDE worksheet tied to the trust boundaries of one design.
entries.when_to_use: Use before calling a design ready to build, once the component sketch exists.
